Finding a name

Can typo-tolerant search help first-year commuters find a campus service they can’t quite spell, while keeping familiar searches predictable?

Audience and scope

Audience. First-year commuter students who need to find a campus office or service between classes.

Dream. Make a campus directory that helps a new commuter find the right office from a half-remembered name and keep a short list for later.

Working promise. Create an account and sign in, find a service by name or category, bookmark it, reopen it from a private dashboard, and update a display name or password before signing out.

Assumptions to test. A small curated catalog can run in the browser. Students often remember part of a name. A plausible wrong match could send someone to the wrong service. The current prototype uses fictional names to isolate search behavior.

Two project concepts

Campus resource finder

Search a small catalog of campus services and save one bookmark per resource. The private dashboard shows a count and recent bookmarks.

First screen · Find a campus service → Search → Matching services

Between-class study planner

Choose a subject and a 15-, 25-, or 45-minute study block. Save the plan and see recent plans and total planned minutes in a private dashboard.

First screen · Choose a subject → Pick a duration → Save plan

Choice. Build the resource finder. Its search and bookmark flow builds on the existing lookup prototype. The planner would have simpler matching rules but would test time planning instead of search quality.

Presentation choice. Lead with search for commuters who have a service in mind. A browse-first layout organized by category would suit orientation students discovering what exists. Keep category labels in the search results and ask a partner whether the search entry point is clear.

Five stories

These are the expected checks for the planned application.

  1. 1. Join and return I can register and sign in. A duplicate username and incorrect password each produce an error.
  2. 2. Find and bookmark a service I can search by name or category and save a valid result. Empty searches prompt for a term, unknown resource IDs are rejected, and saving twice leaves one bookmark.
  3. 3. Reopen my saved resources I see an empty state on a new account, then my bookmark count and recent links. Data survives a new session and a restart. A second account cannot read or change my bookmarks.
  4. 4. Maintain my account I can edit my display name and change my password after entering the current one. The old password fails, other sessions lose access, and the current session continues.
  5. 5. Leave safely I can sign out. A later request to the dashboard or bookmark action requires sign-in.

Architecture sketch

Planned stack. Python with Django 5.2, Django templates and forms, a small JavaScript search module, and SQLite. Django supplies authentication and session handling. SQLite fits a local build with a small catalog and a few test accounts.

  1. Browser Render the public catalog and search it locally. Submit the selected resource ID to bookmark it.
  2. Django server Require a session and a CSRF token for saving. Look up the resource ID and take ownership from the signed-in account. Filter dashboard queries to that owner.
  3. SQLite database Store users, resources and bookmarks. A unique owner and resource pair keeps repeated saves from adding duplicates.

The server renders the count and recent bookmarks from persisted rows. Account edits apply to the signed-in user. Use Django’s password change form and verify session behavior with two browser sessions.

Two search approaches

Normalized substring

Trim spaces, use lowercase and Unicode NFC, then look for the same character sequence inside each name. This is the baseline. Its behavior is easy to explain and reproduce, but it misses spelling errors.

Fuse.js fuzzy ranking

Score approximate matches and rank candidates. The documentation shows that fuzzy matching is available. How well it handles similar names and unrelated inputs here is an open question.

Decision. Keep literal matching as the first pass. If the experiment supports it, offer fuzzy candidates as possible matches only after an empty result. The student chooses the service to save.

Baseline checks

Observed. Five fixed assertions passed locally on November 11, 2026. The baseline missed the transposed name as expected. That result motivates the experiment.

Planned. Use synthetic accounts to test sign-in, duplicate saves, restart persistence, two-user ownership, password changes and logout. See the verification log for what has run.

Next experiment

Planned experiment. Can a labeled “Possible matches” list recover mistyped queries without directing students to the wrong service? Run both approaches on 12 labeled queries with four exact or partial inputs, five typos and three unrelated queries. Include two similar catalog entries. Record the order of returned IDs against the expected IDs written before testing.

Pass and stop rule. Add the fallback only if at least four of five typos place the intended entry in the top three, all four literal results keep their order, and no more than one unrelated query returns suggestions. If a 45-minute trial misses those thresholds or the ranking is unclear, keep literal search with a prompt to try a shorter term. The fuzzy comparison is pending.

Pattern trial. Compare one search function with a conditional against two small search functions with a shared result format. Run the same query checks and see whether the second design lets the fallback change independently without making the result harder to trace.

Partner task. Open the Fuse.js source, explain the fallback choice, try Chen and Jodran, and identify one assumption or confusing step. The walkthrough is pending. Peer review issue

Sources and AI use

  • ECMAScript · checked November 12, 2026. Substring inclusion checks for a literal sequence. NFC normalizes equivalent Unicode representations, which explains the decomposed-accent test. Substring inclusion · Unicode normalization
  • Fuse.js · checked November 12, 2026. The project documents approximate matching and a result score. That supports testing a suggestions list. Fuse.js documentation
  • Django · checked November 12, 2026. The auth docs describe password hashing and how password changes affect sessions. The CSRF guide shows how to protect internal POST forms. Both inform the account and bookmark checks. Django authentication · Django CSRF guidance
  • SQLite · checked November 12, 2026. SQLite documents a local storage model and a tradeoff for concurrent writers. A single local app is the planned scope. SQLite use cases

AI helped draft the alternatives, fixture and test plan. The baseline was executed against expected results and technical claims were checked against the original docs. Search quality on service names and the planned account journey still need testing.
